policy: Separate daily homework is not routinely assigned. This is optional practice for families who want a regular routine. Choose what is useful; there is no expectation to complete the whole menu or submit optional practice.
unfinished: Check your planner and the instructions Mr. Wyatt has given you. Finish only the small piece identified for you, using the support agreed at school. An unfinished class activity is not automatically homework. If you were absent or are unsure, ask where to begin.
routine: Read or listen for 10–15 minutes, then choose one short activity. Families wanting a longer routine can add a second choice, keeping the total around 30–40 minutes including reading, or less when needed. Spread choices across evenings or select a few for the weekend; do not save up a catch-up pile.
stopRule: Stop if the work is confusing, upsetting or taking much longer than expected. Let Mr. Wyatt know which part was difficult. Rest, play, family time and activities outside school matter too.
access: Use paper, drawings, spoken explanations or a language that helps you think. Every menu activity can be done without an online account. No purchase, AI tool or routine portfolio upload is required.

week.label: Read, practise factor trees and create
week.connection: This week’s optional choices connect to reading, the factor trees we are using in class, and explaining creative choices. Pick one that is useful. These are not new assignments, and there is no routine upload or hand-in deadline.

activities.subject: Math
activities.title: Factor trees or a familiar fact family
activities.context: Optional practice · factor trees are being used in class
activities.example: For 12, split 12 = 3 × 4, then 4 = 2 × 2. The prime end factors are 2, 2 and 3. Keep both 2s: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. A prime number has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself; 1 is not prime.
steps: Choose 18 or 24. Draw a factor tree, splitting composite numbers until every end number is prime.
Write all the prime end factors, including repeats, and multiply them to check your starting number.
Prefer a familiar fact family? Use 3 × 6 = 18 to say or write 6 × 3 = 18, 18 ÷ 3 = 6 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3. Explain how the same three numbers are connected.
activities.check: 18 = 2 × 3 × 3. 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3. A different tree can be correct if it ends in the same prime factors and multiplies back to the starting number. In the fact-family option, multiplication and division undo each other.
activities.extension: Try a second tree for the same number using a different first split. Explain what changes and what stays the same.

activities.subject: Math
activities.title: Compare and explain
activities.example: 4.7 = 4.70. Compare 4.70 and 4.65: the ones are equal, but 7 tenths is greater than 6 tenths, so 4.7 > 4.65. Extra decimal digits do not automatically make a number larger.
steps: Compare 48,305 and 48,350 using <, > or =. Start at the greatest place value and find the first differing digit.
Compare 0.8 and 0.75, then 3.04 and 3.4. Explain with place value, a drawing or a number line.
Put 2.5, 2.05 and 2.50 in order from least to greatest. Explain any equality.
activities.check: 48,305 < 48,350; 0.8 > 0.75; 3.04 < 3.4; 2.05 < 2.5 = 2.50. Explain the value of the first differing digit, rather than counting digits.
activities.extension: Choose two different decimals that both round to 3.5 to the nearest tenth. Compare the original numbers and explain why their rounded values match.

activities.subject: Language Arts
activities.title: Read, notice and explain
activities.context: Connects to reading and listening routines
activities.example: Try: ‘I think the character is worried because they keep checking the door.’ For nonfiction: ‘The main idea is … One detail is …’
steps: Read or listen to a short part of a book you choose.
Tell, draw or write one important event or idea.
Point to one detail that supports your idea. Could the same detail suggest another reasonable interpretation? For nonfiction, name something the text does not tell you.
activities.check: Can someone follow your explanation and find the detail? Different interpretations can work when the text supports them. A spoken answer counts.

activities.subject: Language Arts
activities.title: Tell a tiny mystery
activities.context: Connects to storytelling and reasoning in Werewolf
activities.example: A library book disappears. A bookmark is on the sofa and a book-shaped lump is under a cushion. The reader finds it there.
steps: Invent a missing-object mystery with a beginning, problem and ending.
Tell it in about one minute. Include two clues.
Ask which clue helped your listener; retell one part more clearly. You can practise alone or with a toy.
activities.check: Does the ending fit both clues? Did you keep imagined details separate from real events?

activities.subject: Social Studies
activities.title: Make a game fairer
activities.context: Connects to games and our classroom community
activities.example: Allow a practice round before scoring so a beginner can learn the rules.
steps: Choose a familiar game. Explain one rule and whom it helps.
Imagine a new player cannot join in easily. Suggest one change.
Explain how your change helps people participate.
activities.check: Name who benefits and explain why. Could your change create a different problem? Revise it if needed.

activities.subject: Science
activities.title: Notice before you guess
activities.context: General observation practice · no new science unit assigned
activities.example: ‘The leaf has a brown edge’ is an observation. ‘It may have dried out’ is a possible explanation.
steps: Choose a safe everyday object, such as a spoon or leaf.
Draw it and write three things you can directly observe.
Write one question and one possible explanation. Label the explanation ‘I think …’.
activities.check: Can you separate what you observed from what you think caused it? Do not taste unknown objects or plants.

activities.subject: French
activities.title: Use words you already know
activities.context: Review only · use familiar classroom words
activities.example: If familiar: bonjour = hello; merci = thank you; au revoir = goodbye.
steps: Choose three French words or phrases you have already learned.
Say each one and match it to a picture or meaning.
Cover your notes and try again. If none are familiar yet, skip this choice.
activities.check: Can you match each phrase to its meaning without looking? Check classroom notes; ask at school about pronunciation.

activities.subject: Arts Education
activities.title: Draw the same object twice
activities.example: A mug handle may appear on the side in one view and be hidden in the other.
steps: Draw a safe everyday object from the front.
Turn it or move your seat and draw it from another angle.
Circle one detail that changed and one that stayed the same.
activities.check: Can someone tell the drawings show different views? Explain one choice of line or shape.

activities.subject: ADST
activities.title: Build, test and improve
activities.example: Fold a sheet into a tent. If it tips, try a wider base.
steps: Use one sheet of scrap paper to make a freestanding name card. Keep it at home.
Test whether it stands for ten seconds.
Change one fold and test again. Draw or describe what improved.
activities.check: What did you change? Did the second version stand more steadily? An unsuccessful test still gives useful information.

activities.subject: Physical and Health Education
activities.title: Move in a way that works for you
activities.context: Connects to active play and shared rules
activities.example: Try three favourite movements with pauses between them.
steps: Choose a walk, dance, stretch or comfortable seated movement.
Choose a safe space and a pace that feels manageable.
Notice how you feel before and after.
activities.check: Describe how your body felt and one choice that helped you move safely. There is no speed or distance target.

activities.subject: Career Education
activities.title: Prepare for tomorrow
activities.example: ‘I can pack my book. I need help finding the form.’
steps: Check your planner or the reminder you were given.
Choose one useful task: pack a book, organize supplies or put a form where an adult will see it.
Name one thing you can do independently and one thing you need help with.
activities.check: Can you find the item you need? Choose one small next step; do not share private family information.

districtResources.intro: Optional choices from Surrey Schools ONE’s approved digital-resource directory. Approval conditions vary by resource; these are not extra assignments or a claim that every account is ready.
districtResources.access: Open a Surrey listing below for its Visit Website link and current access steps. For district passwords, use PASSWORDS → Parent/Student on Surrey Schools ONE; that area asks for a Surrey Schools sign-in. Never post passwords here. If school access or consent is not ready, ask Mr. Wyatt and use the screen-free choice. No purchase is needed.

items.title: Sora
items.subject: Reading & listening
items.description: Borrow ebooks and audiobooks through the school reading service. Surrey’s listing directs students to sign in with their Surrey Schools email and password.
items.activity: Read or listen for 10–15 minutes. Retell one part and explain a detail that stood out.
items.offline: Read a book or comic you have, or listen to someone tell a story.

items.title: Math Learning Center apps
items.subject: Math · visual models
items.description: Use the free virtual manipulatives to show familiar maths. Surrey’s approval covers the apps, not the learning resources sold in the store.
items.activity: Model 243 as 2 hundreds, 4 tens and 3 ones. Show another way: 1 hundred, 14 tens and 3 ones. Explain why the value stays the same.
items.offline: Draw and label the hundreds, tens and ones on paper.

items.title: World Book Student
items.subject: Research · Grade 5+
items.description: An encyclopedia with articles, images and read-aloud support. Surrey lists conditional approval requiring a signed Technology Tool Consent form. Use the district access steps, not a paid personal subscription.
items.activity: Choose one question about a familiar topic. Read a short article, write two facts in your own words and record the article title.
items.offline: Use a nonfiction book, or write your question to bring to school.

items.title: Explora Primary
items.subject: Research · Grades 4–7
items.description: Surrey’s Grades 4–7 research database, with text and read-aloud options. Its conditional approval requires a signed Technology Tool Consent form and district access.
items.activity: Search a familiar science or social studies topic. Explain one new fact and record the title of the source where you found it.
items.offline: Read a nonfiction page you already have. Share a fact and point to its source.

items.title: Learn360
items.subject: Science & other subjects
items.description: Educational videos, audio and learning materials. Surrey’s conditional approval requires a signed Technology Tool Consent form. Follow the student access steps on the listing.
items.activity: With an adult, choose a short clip about a familiar topic. Pause and explain two things you learned and one question you still have.
items.offline: Draw a familiar object and label two observations and one question.

items.title: Curio (CBC)
items.subject: Canadian stories · English & French
items.description: CBC video and audio resources. Surrey requires a signed Technology Tool Consent form and an account; its published sign-in steps are labelled for teachers. Ask Mr. Wyatt about student access before creating an account.
items.activity: Once access is confirmed, choose an age-appropriate short item with an adult. Retell its main idea and explain one supporting detail.
items.offline: Discuss a story or community event with an adult. Separate what you know from what you wonder.

resources.title: Matific
resources.subject: Math · extra practice & challenge
resources.description: Optional extra maths practice and challenge using your school-provided account once access is working. Try a short session of around 10–15 minutes. Students who would like to work ahead may explore more challenging activities available in their account when ready. Explain your thinking and ask for help if a new idea is confusing. There is no required score, weekly target or extra submission. You do not need to buy a subscription or create a separate account.
resources.offline: Try the factor-tree or fact-family choice above, or compare numbers from the reusable menu. If you cannot sign in, use this option and ask Mr. Wyatt at school.

resources.title: Prodigy Math
resources.subject: Math
resources.description: Use school-provided login details when available. Choose familiar maths or practice your teacher identifies. A paid membership is not required for this menu.
resources.offline: Use the factor-tree or familiar fact-family choice above, or explain a familiar problem on paper.

resources.title: NoRedInk
resources.subject: Language Arts
resources.description: Use class instructions and account details supplied by your teacher. If access is not ready or no practice is listed, choose reading or storytelling.
resources.offline: Write three sentences about your reading. Check capitals, sentence endings and whether each sentence makes sense.

resources.title: Reading in any language
resources.subject: Language Arts
resources.description: Choose a book, comic or other text you have, or listen to someone read. Discuss one idea and the detail that supports it.
resources.offline: Use a book at home or a borrowed classroom or library book.

resources.title: Math Antics
resources.subject: Math
resources.description: Optional explanation videos. Choose Prime Factorization to revisit the factor trees we are using, or a familiar topic such as Rounding. The written example above is enough to begin; no worksheet subscription is needed.
resources.offline: Use the written factor-tree model and checking guidance above. No video, account or purchase is needed.

resources.title: Truth and Reconciliation family guide
resources.subject: Social Studies
resources.description: For families when this learning begins in class. Preview the selected sources and follow your child’s readiness. Conversation is optional.
resources.offline: Ask what your child would like to share from class. They may pass; no separate research or submission is expected.

resources.title: Rights and expression family guide
resources.subject: Social Studies
resources.description: An optional connection to our rights and belonging resources. Follow classroom timing; this is not extra assigned research.
resources.offline: Discuss how a familiar game or shared space could include people fairly. Use a fictional example.

familyCheck: Ask: ‘What did you try, and why?’
Notice one thing your child did independently and one place they needed help.
Use checking guidance after an attempt. Correct together without turning optional practice into a test.
Keep notes at home. Contact Mr. Wyatt privately about persistent difficulty; do not post names, scores or work on this public site.
